latin: Sicut caracteres sunt proprii operi magico, ita numeri sunt proprii operi cabalae, medio existente inter utrosque et appropriabili per declinationem ad extrema usu litterarum.
translation: Just as characters are proper to the work of magic, so numbers are proper to the work of Cabala, with a middle existing between the two, appropriable to either extreme by declination through the use of letters.
translation_note: 'caracteres' (characters) means magical words in general rather than figures on astrological talismans, as Farmer argues against Frances Yates's reading (farmer1998:25541).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch1, from Latin at farmer1998:25475
doctrine: Farmer glosses 'characters' as magical words in general, explicitly rejecting Frances Yates's view that the term refers to words inscribed on astrological talismans (farmer1998:25541). Pico's point, per Farmer, is that magical words can be translated into numbers and numbers into magical words, apparently through the word-number equations of gematria, and that the 'works' in view are those of contemplative or prophetic magic, as in the two preceding theses (farmer1998:25541).
context: Farmer cross-references the thesis to five others: 11>12, on the impossibility of operating through pure Cabala without a rationally intellectual nature; 1>6, on the Thomist-Scotist distinction ex natura rei; 9>16 through 9>18, on the nature that is the 'horizon' of time and eternity and its relation to the magician; and 9>26, contrasting the effect of a pure and immediate Cabalistic work with what no magic can attain (farmer1998:26604; farmer1998:18596; farmer1998:25354; farmer1998:25358; farmer1998:25362; farmer1998:25480).
historiography: Akopyan quotes the thesis together with its immediate predecessor (9>24) in a discussion of the relation between formal number and magical and Cabalistic operation (akopyan2018:618; akopyan2021:1347). Busi's edition and commentary situate the thesis among the magical conclusions and their restriction to natural magic (busi2014:1667; busi2014:9639). Wirszubski cites the thesis's Latin as evidence that "linguistic symbolism to numerical symbolism which makes itself felt throughout the translations of Mithridates is reflected in Pico's theses" (wirszubski1989:4353), and elsewhere calls it Pico's "twenty-fifth magical thesis" (wirszubski1989:7158). Howlett quotes and translates it, citing Farmer's edition directly (howlett2021:6198).
